Fix \((P,m_0,m_1,p)\in\mathcal M_n\) and \(0<\lambda\leq\lambda _0\).  By ass:positivity,
\[
 \{0<e(X)\leq\lambda\}
 =\mathop{\dot\bigcup}_{j=0}^{\infty}
 \{2^{-j-1}\lambda<e(X)\leq2^{-j}\lambda\}
 \, P\text{-almost surely}.
\]
The upper half of ass:uniform-shell and countable additivity therefore give
\[
 P\{e(X)\leq\lambda\}
 \leq c_+\lambda^\kappa\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}2^{-j\kappa}
 ={c_+\over1-2^{-\kappa}}\lambda^\kappa.
\]
The shell with upper endpoint \(\lambda\), together with the lower half of ass:uniform-shell, gives
\[
 P\{e(X)\leq\lambda\}\geq
 P\{\lambda/2<e(X)\leq\lambda\}\geq c_-\lambda^\kappa.
\]
This proves the first uniform equivalence, including its support premise.

Put \(H_\lambda=E_P[(e(X)\vee\lambda)^{-1}]\).  Its part below \(\lambda\) is bounded above and below by constant multiples of \(\lambda^{\kappa-1}\):
\[
 c_-\lambda^{\kappa-1}
 \leq {P\{e(X)\leq\lambda\}\over\lambda}
 \leq {c_+\over1-2^{-\kappa}}\lambda^{\kappa-1}.
\]
For the part above \(\lambda\), let \(J\) be the largest integer for which \(2^J\lambda\leq\lambda _0\).  On the shell
\(2^j\lambda<e(X)\leq2^{j+1}\lambda\), inverse propensity is at most \((2^j\lambda)^{-1}\).  Assumption ass:uniform-shell, with upper endpoint \(2^{j+1}\lambda\), implies
\[
 E_P\!\left[{\mathbf 1\{2^j\lambda<e(X)\leq2^{j+1}\lambda\}\over e(X)}\right]
 \leq 2c_+(2^{j+1}\lambda)^{\kappa-1}.
\]
The possible terminal shell and the event \(e(X)>\lambda _0\) contribute at most a constant depending only on \((c_+,\kappa,\lambda _0)\).  Consequently,
\[
 H_\lambda\leq C\left[1+\lambda^{\kappa-1}
 \sum_{j=0}^{J}2^{j(\kappa-1)}\right].
\]
If \(0<\kappa<1\), the geometric sum is bounded and the first lower display proves
\(H_\lambda\asymp\lambda^{\kappa-1}\).  If \(\kappa=1\), each complete shell between \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda _0\) contributes at least
\[
 {1\over2^{j+1}\lambda}
 P\{2^j\lambda<e(X)\leq2^{j+1}\lambda\}\geq c_-/2,
\]
while the preceding upper bound gives a constant per shell.  Since \(J+1\asymp1+\log(\lambda _0/\lambda)\), this proves
\(H_\lambda\asymp1+\log(\lambda _0/\lambda)\).  If \(\kappa>1\), the upper geometric sum is bounded by a constant; a fixed shell, for example the shell with upper endpoint \(\lambda _0\), gives the positive constant lower bound
\[
 H_\lambda\geq \lambda _0^{-1}P\{\lambda _0/2<e(X)\leq\lambda _0\}
 \geq c_-\lambda _0^{\kappa-1}.
\]
These three cases are precisely \(H_\lambda\asymp v_\kappa(\lambda)^2\).  Every constant used above is independent of \(P\), \(n\), and \(\lambda\), as required.

We prove the claim against the corrected construction proposed for def:median-estimator.  If \(n\geq5\), its five nonempty blocks are independent by ass:iid, and each block statistic is measurable in its block and the deterministic public inputs.  The median is a Borel function of five real numbers.  If \(1\leq n<5\), the corrected construction uses the measurable full-sample clipped statistic.  Thus def:estimator-class implies \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{med}}\in\mathcal T_n\) in both cases.

Now let \(n\geq5\), let \(Z_j=\widehat\tau_{\lambda_n^\star}^{(j)}-\tau(P)\), and put \(a=K\rho_n\).  The premise and Markov's inequality give \(P(|Z_j|>u)\leq a/u\).  If the median has absolute error greater than \(u\), at least three of the five events \(\{|Z_j|>u\}\) occur.  Independence and a union bound over the \({5\choose3}=10\) triples therefore yield
\[
 P\{|\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{med}}-\tau(P)|>u\}
 \leq\min\{1,10(a/u)^3\}.                                    \tag{15}
\]
For any nonnegative random variable \(W\), Tonelli's theorem applied to \(W^2=\int_0^W2u\,du\) gives \(E[W^2]=\int_0^\infty2uP(W>u)\,du\).  Applying this identity to the median error and using the bound \(1\) on \((0,a)\) and the bound \(10(a/u)^3\) on \((a,\infty)\),
\[
 E_P(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{med}}-\tau(P))^2
 \leq\int_0^a2u\,du+\int_a^\infty20a^3u^{-2}\,du
 =21a^2.
\]
Taking square roots proves the stated constant \(\sqrt{21}\).  For later use, when \(n\geq5\), applying the proof of thm:clipped-absolute-upper on a block of size between \(\lfloor n/5\rfloor\) and \(\lceil n/5\rceil\), with the same full-sample threshold, changes only fixed numerical constants in (8)--(13).  Thus its premise holds uniformly with a class-constant \(K\).  When \(1\leq n<5\), \(\lambda_n^\star\geq\min\{\lambda_0,4^{-1/(\kappa+1)}\}>0\).  Assumptions ass:outcome-second-moment and ass:right-overlap imply \(\|g_0\|_{P,2}^2\leq M_Y/\eta_+\), and ass:bounded-treatment-effect-signal then bounds \(\|g_1\|_{P,2}\).  The public-radius assumptions bound \(\|m_0\|_{P,2}\) and \(\|m_1\|_{P,2}\).  Substitution in the score of def:clipped-score therefore gives a class-constant second-moment bound, while \(\rho_n\geq n^{-1/2}\geq1/2\).  Hence the corrected full-sample fallback satisfies
\[
 \sup_{\mathcal M_n}\{E_P(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{med}}-\tau(P))^2\}^{1/2}\leq C\rho_n,
 \,1\leq n<5.                                             \tag{15a}
\]

We prove the proposed, well-posed version, in which \(\mathcal M_n\) is nonempty.  This qualification is necessary: a positive minimax lower bound over an empty class is false.  Nonemptiness and the lower shell inequality at \(u=\lambda _0\), together with ass:right-overlap, imply
\[
 1-\eta_+>\lambda _0/2.                                      \tag{16}
\]

We first record the elementary testing inequality used for every channel.  If two sample laws \(Q_+,Q_-\) have targets \(t_+,t_-\) with \(|t_+-t_-|\geq2d\), the two events \(\{|T-t_+|<d\}\) and \(\{|T-t_-|<d\}\) are disjoint.  The definition of total variation then gives
\[
 Q_+\{|T-t_+|\geq d\}+Q_-\{|T-t_-|\geq d\}
 \geq1-\operatorname{TV}(Q_+,Q_-).                           \tag{17}
\]
Thus one error probability is at least half the right-hand side.  The same proof applies to two priors: if their mixture sample laws have total variation at most \(\gamma\) and their random targets lie within \(d/4\) of two centers separated by \(2d\), except on prior probability \(\epsilon\), then every estimator has error at least \(d/2\) with probability at least \((1-\gamma-2\epsilon)/2\) under one mixture.  This follows by using the estimator to test which center is closer and applying (17).  Because a mixture error probability is an average of fixed-law error probabilities, the resulting supremum is attained or exceeded by a fixed law in the prior support.

Here is a common class-valid reservoir construction.  Put \(L=1-\eta_+\), and choose \(a\in(\lambda _0/2,L)\), possible by (16).  On a background reservoir use propensity values \(a_j=a2^{-j}\), \(j\geq0\).  Give \(a_0\) mass \(w_0=c_-\lambda _0^\kappa\), and, for \(j\geq1\), give \(a_j\) mass
\[
 w_j=c_-a_{j-1}^\kappa.                                      \tag{18a}
\]
For \(0<u<a\), exactly one dyadic point \(a_j\) lies in \((u/2,u]\); if \(u\in[a_j,a_{j-1})\), its mass satisfies
\[
 c_-u^\kappa\leq w_j\leq2^\kappa c_-u^\kappa.               \tag{18b}
\]
For \(a\leq u\leq\lambda _0<2a\), the top atom belongs to the shell and \(w_0=c_-\lambda _0^\kappa\geq c_-u^\kappa\).  Moreover,
\[
 \sum_{j\geq0}w_j
 =c_-\lambda _0^\kappa+{c_-a^\kappa\over1-2^{-\kappa}}
 <{1-2^{-\kappa}\over4}+{1\over4}<1/2                     \tag{18c}
\]
by ass:lower-shell-richness.  Assumptions ass:lower-shell-richness and ass:upper-shell-richness also imply \(2^\kappa c_-<c_+\).  Thus (18b), with the top-atom bound \(w_0<1/4\leq c_+u^\kappa\) for \(u\geq a>\lambda _0/2\), proves the two shell inequalities for the background reservoir.  Add a second, sufficiently small active reservoir with dyadic propensity values below \(s_0\) and masses proportional to their \(\kappa\)-powers, where
\[
 0<s_0<\min\{a,L/4,\lambda _0/4\}.                            \tag{18}
\]
The ratio between the richness upper and lower constants leaves a fixed positive slack, so the active-reservoir weight can be chosen such that every propensity perturbation by a factor in \([1/2,2]\) still satisfies the two shell inequalities.  Put all remaining probability on two regular cells having the same propensity \(p_*\in(\lambda _0,L)\) when that interval is nonempty, and otherwise at a point of \((a,L)\) whose mass is included in the preceding upper-bound slack.  Geometric summation of (18a) and its active-reservoir analogue proves, uniformly in every perturbation below,
\[
 c_-u^\kappa\leq P\{u/2<e(X)\leq u\}\leq c_+u^\kappa,
 \,0<u\leq\lambda _0.                                   \tag{19}
\]
The construction uses only countably many covariate points, including finitely many cell refinements at each \(n\), and therefore embeds measurably in every infinite standard Borel \(\mathcal X\).  A nonempty class cannot have finite \(\mathcal X\), because ass:positivity and the lower shell inequality require infinitely many positive propensity values tending to zero.

For every family below, take \(D\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(e(X))\), let the potential outcomes be conditionally independent of \(D\) given \(X\), and set \(Y=DY_1+(1-D)Y_0\).  This proves ass:consistency and ass:ignorability; (18)--(19) prove positivity, the shell law, and right overlap.  Use centered Gaussian treated noise with variance \(0<\sigma^2\leq\sigma_1^2\wedge M_Y/4\) when a Kullback--Leibler calculation is needed, and zero residuals otherwise.  Multiply all displayed regression amplitudes by one sufficiently small fixed constant \(c_A>0\).  Since the radii are bounded by \(\bar r\), choose \(c_A\) so that
\[
 E_P[(g_1-g_0)^2]\leq M,\; E_P[Y^2]\leq M_Y             \tag{20}
\]
in every family.  This calibration changes only class-constant factors and proves the two moment memberships rather than assuming them.

We now construct the channels.  First, the root-\(n\) floor uses the two regular cells.  Keep their common propensity and all conditional outcome laws fixed, set a known treatment-effect signal equal to \(+c_A\) on one cell and \(-c_A\) on the other, and move probability \(c_A/\sqrt n\) from one cell to the other under the two hypotheses.  The public functions equal the true nuisances and are identical under both laws.  The one-row Kullback--Leibler divergence is at most \(C/n\), the product divergence is at most \(C\), and choosing \(c_A\) smaller makes product total variation at most \(1/4\) by the elementary inequality \(\operatorname{TV}^2\leq\mathrm{KL}/2\), whose proof follows from \((\sqrt x-1)^2\leq(x-1)\log x/2\) and Cauchy--Schwarz.  The target separation is \(c/\sqrt n\).  Equation (17) gives the first obstruction.

For \(0<\kappa<1\), suppose first that
\(s=(nr_{1n}^2)^{-1}\leq s_0\).  On the active set \(A_s=\{e\leq s\}\), whose mass \(m_s\) satisfies \(m_s\asymp s^\kappa\) by geometric summation, take
\[
 m_1=0,\, p=e,\, g_{1,\pm}=\pm h\mathbf 1_{A_s},
 \, h={c_A r_{1n}\over\sqrt{m_s}},                       \tag{21}
\]
and take the control regression and its public version equal to zero.  Then \(\|m_1-g_{1,\pm}\|_2=c_A r_{1n}\leq r_{1n}\).  Geometric summation gives \(m_s\asymp s^\kappa\) and \(E[e\mathbf 1_{A_s}]\leq Csm_s\).  Gaussian mean-shift calculus gives
\[
 \mathrm{KL}(P_+^n,P_-^n)
 ={2nh^2\over\sigma^2}E[e(X)\mathbf 1_{A_s}]
 \leq Cnh^2s m_s\leq Cc_A^2,                                \tag{22}
\]
whereas
\[
 |\tau(P_+)-\tau(P_-)|=2hm_s\asymp r_{1n}s^{\kappa/2}
 =n^{-\kappa/2}r_{1n}^{1-\kappa}.                            \tag{23}
\]
If \(s>s_0\), this last expression is at most a class-constant multiple of \(n^{-1/2}\), so the root-\(n\) family covers it.

At \(\kappa=1\), put \(s=(nr_{1n}^2)^{-1}\) and, when \(s<s_0/2\), set
\[
 g_{1,\pm}=\pm {a_n\over e}\mathbf 1\{s\leq e\leq s_0\},
 \, a_n={c_A\over\sqrt{n\{1+\log(s_0/s)\}}}.            \tag{24}
\]
The active atomic masses are proportional to the propensity values when \(\kappa=1\).  Summing the dyadic levels between \(s\) and \(s_0\) therefore gives
\[
 \|g_{1,\pm}\|_2^2\leq Ca_n^2/s\leq Cc_A^2r_{1n}^2,
 \,
 \mathrm{KL}(P_+^n,P_-^n)\leq Cna_n^2\log(s_0/s)\leq Cc_A^2,\tag{25}
\]
and
\[
 |\tau(P_+)-\tau(P_-)|
 \geq c a_n\log(s_0/s)
 \asymp n^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+\log_+(nr_{1n}^2)}.                  \tag{26}
\]
When the interval in (24) is empty or has bounded logarithmic length, the root-\(n\) family supplies (26).  For \(\kappa>1\), \(Q_\kappa=n^{-1/2}\), already supplied by that family.  Equations (21)--(26) prove the full \(Q_\kappa\) channel.

For the empty-treatment channel take \(s=c_sn^{-1/(\kappa+1)}\leq s_0\), with \(c_s>0\) small, and use (21) on \(A_s\).  Couple the two samples identically unless some observation lies in \(A_s\) and is treated.  By a union bound and direct tail integration,
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_+^n,P_-^n)
 \leq nP\{X\in A_s,D=1\}
 \leq Cns^{\kappa+1}\leq Cc_s^{\kappa+1}.                   \tag{27}
\]
The target separation is
\[
 2hm_s\asymp r_{1n}s^{\kappa/2}
 \asymp r_{1n}n^{-\kappa/[2(\kappa+1)]}.                     \tag{28}
\]
Choose \(c_s\) so that (27) is at most \(1/4\).  If the required \(s\) exceeds \(s_0\), then \(n\) is bounded by a class constant and the root-\(n\) family, with the amplitude calibration (20), covers (28).

For the weak-tail nuisance product, first take
\(s=c_s r_{en}^{2/(\kappa+2)}\leq s_0/2\), let
\(B_s=\{s<e\leq2s\}\) in the active reservoir, and write \(m=P(B_s)\asymp s^\kappa\).  Partition an auxiliary coordinate into \(N\) equiprobable cells.  Under hypothesis \(\theta\in\{-1,1\}\), draw independent cell signs with
\[
 \Pr_\theta(Z_j=z)={1+\theta\delta z\over2},\, z\in\{-1,1\},
\]
where \(0<\delta<1/4\) is fixed, and for every fixed sign vector set
\[
 m_1=0,\, p=e_0,\, g_1=hZ_j\mathbf 1_{B_s},\,
 e_{\theta,Z}={e_0\over1+\theta\delta Z_j},\;
 h={c_A r_{1n}\over\sqrt m}.                                 \tag{29}
\]
The public triple is identical under both hypotheses.  Moreover,
\[
 \|m_1-g_1\|_2=c_A r_{1n},\,
 \|p-e_{\theta,Z}\|_2\leq C\delta s\sqrt m
 \leq r_{en}                                                   \tag{30}
\]
after fixing \(c_s\), and (19)--(20) prove membership of every fixed-sign law.  For a row in a previously unseen cell,
\[
 \Pr_\theta(Z_j=z)e_{\theta,Z}
 ={1+\theta\delta z\over2}{e_0\over1+\theta\delta z}
 ={e_0\over2}.                                                 \tag{31}
\]
Thus both the treated row, including its outcome distribution, and the summed control row have the same one-row mixture law for \(\theta=1\) and \(\theta=-1\).  The sample mixtures can differ only if two observations from \(B_s\) use the same cell.  Hence
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(\overline P_+^n,\overline P_-^n)
 \leq {n(n-1)\over2N}.                                       \tag{32}
\]
Under either prior,
\[
 \tau(P_{\theta,Z})=hmN^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N Z_j,\;
 E_\theta\tau(P_{\theta,Z})=\theta\delta hm,\;
 \operatorname{Var}_\theta\{\tau(P_{\theta,Z})\}
 \leq {h^2m^2\over N}.                                       \tag{33}
\]
Take \(N\geq n^3\) and then enlarge its fixed multiplier so that (32) and the Chebyshev failure probability in (33) are each at most \(1/16\).  The prior version of (17) gives an error of order
\[
 hm\asymp r_{1n}s^{\kappa/2}\asymp
 r_{1n}r_{en}^{\kappa/(\kappa+2)}.                            \tag{34}
\]
If the proposed \(s\) exceeds \(s_0/2\), use the fixed shell \(s_0/4<e\leq s_0/2\).  The propensity certificate is then feasible because \(r_{en}\) is bounded below, and the separation is \(c r_{1n}\), which dominates (34) up to a constant because \(r_{en}\leq\bar r\).

For the control product, use a regular region of fixed mass \(m_*>0\), partition it into \(N\) cells, and put
\[
 g_0=h_0Z_j,\; m_0=0,\;
 1-e_{\theta,Z}={1-p_*\over1+\theta tZ_j},\; p=p_*,\;
 h_0={c_A r_{0n}\over\sqrt{m_*}},\;
 t=c_A\min\{r_{en}/\sqrt{m_*},1/4\}.                          \tag{35}
\]
Bias the sign prior by \(\Pr_\theta(Z_j=z)=(1+\theta tz)/2\).  The analogue of (31) now cancels the control row, while the treated row is unchanged because its outcome is zero.  Every fixed law satisfies
\(\|m_0-g_0\|_2\leq r_{0n}\) and \(\|p-e\|_2\leq r_{en}\).  The collision and concentration calculations (32)--(33) give separation \(c r_{0n}r_{en}\) when \(r_{en}\) is small and \(c r_{0n}\) otherwise; boundedness by \(\bar r\) makes the latter at least a class-constant multiple of \(r_{0n}r_{en}\).

We have thus produced, inside \(\mathcal M_n\), fixed-law or fuzzy subexperiments with probability separation bounded below by a universal positive number for each of
\[
 Q_\kappa(n,r_{1n}),\,
 r_{1n}n^{-\kappa/[2(\kappa+1)]},\,
 r_{1n}r_{en}^{\kappa/(\kappa+2)},\,
 r_{0n}r_{en}.                                                 \tag{36}
\]
All public functions are identical within a subexperiment, so allowing a rule to use them and the certified radii does not alter (17).  Since the sum of four nonnegative numbers is at most four times their maximum, (36) and (17) yield constants \(c>0\) and a probability strictly larger than \(2\delta _0>0\) such that
\[
 \sup_{\mathcal M_n}P\{|T-\tau(P)|\geq c\rho_n\}\geq2\delta _0. \tag{37}
\]
This is stronger than the claimed probability statement.  Finally, on the event in (37), absolute loss is at least \(c\rho_n\) and squared loss at least \(c^2\rho_n^2\).  Taking expectations, then the supremum and infimum specified in def:absolute-risk and def:root-mse-risk, proves
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^{(1)}\geq2c\delta _0\rho_n,\;
 \mathfrak R_n^{(2)}\geq c\sqrt{2\delta _0}\rho_n.
\]
Renaming constants gives the stated consequences.

We prove the proposed version for a nonempty model class.  When \(n\geq5\), the blockwise conclusion in the proof of lem:median-risk-upgrade makes its premise hold with a uniform constant \(K\), and (15) gives
\[
 \sup_{\mathcal M_n}P\{|\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{med}}-\tau(P)|>u\}
 \leq\min\{1,10(K\rho_n/u)^3\}.                              \tag{42}
\]
When \(1\leq n<5\), (15a) and Markov's inequality applied to squared error give the same coverage conclusion after increasing the class-constant multiplier.  Choose \(K_\alpha\) to be the larger of that finite-sample multiplier and \(K(10/\alpha)^{1/3}\).  Then def:bias-aware-interval and (42), with the just-described finite-sample replacement, give
\[
 \inf_{\mathcal M_n}P\{\tau(P)\in\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}\}\geq1-\alpha,
 \,
 \operatorname{length}(\mathcal C_{n,\alpha})=2K_\alpha\rho_n. \tag{43}
\]
The endpoints are measurable in the observed sample and allowed public inputs, so def:interval-rule-class gives \(\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}\in\mathcal I_n\).  Taking expectations in (43) proves the upper length bound.

For the converse, use the channel in the proof of thm:four-channel-converse whose separation is largest.  In a two-point channel, let the targets be separated by \(2d\), with sample total variation at most \(\gamma\).  Honesty gives probability at least \(1-\alpha\) that the interval contains the relevant target under each law.  Transferring one of these events across total variation and intersecting the two events under the other law gives
\[
 P\{\operatorname{length}(C_n)\geq2d\}\geq1-2\alpha-\gamma. \tag{44}
\]
In a fuzzy channel, equations (32)--(33) put the random targets within \(d/4\) of centers separated by \(2d\), except on prior probability \(\epsilon\).  The same event transfer gives
\[
 \overline P\{\operatorname{length}(C_n)\geq3d/2\}
 \geq1-2\alpha-\gamma-2\epsilon.                             \tag{45}
\]
The amplitude, collision multiplier, and concentration multiplier in the converse construction may be chosen so that \(\gamma+2\epsilon<(1-2\alpha)/2\), while changing only the lower-bound constant.  Thus (44) or (45) implies that the mixture expected length is at least \(c_\alpha d\).  A mixture expectation is an average over fixed-sign laws, each of which belongs to \(\mathcal M_n\); hence one fixed law has expected length at least \(c_\alpha d\).  By (36) and the maximum-to-sum comparison, \(d\geq c\rho_n\).  Therefore every honest \(C_n\in\mathcal I_n\) obeys
\[
 \sup_{\mathcal M_n}E_P[\operatorname{length}(C_n)]\geq c_\alpha\rho_n.
\]
Taking the infimum in def:bias-aware-interval and combining with (43) proves \(\mathfrak L_{n,\alpha}\asymp\rho_n\).

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: The corrected median rule \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{med}}\) belongs to \(\mathcal T_n\). If \(n\ge5\) and each of its five independent-block copies of \(\widehat\tau_{\lambda_n^{\star}}\) has mean absolute error at most \(K\rho_n\), then \(P\{|\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{med}}-\tau(P)|>u\}\le\min\{1,10(K\rho_n/u)^3\}\) and \(\{E_P(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{med}}-\tau(P))^2\}^{1/2}\le\sqrt{21}\,K\rho_n\).
proposed_statement_changes.reason: For \(n<5\), a partition into five nonempty blocks does not exist, so the frozen construction's five-copy premise is not well defined. Restricting the amplification assertion to \(n\ge5\), while defining a full-sample fallback for smaller \(n\), is the necessary boundary correction.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: For every admissible radius triple \( (r_{0n},r_{1n},r_{en})\in[0,\bar r]^3 \) for which \(\mathcal M_n\) is nonempty, the handle \(\mathfrak H_{\mathrm{lb}}\) yields constants \(c>0\) and \(\delta_0\in(0,1/4)\), uniform in \(n\), such that every rule \(T\in\mathcal T_n\), including every rule using \(O^{(n)}\), \(m_0\), \(m_1\), \(p\), and the certified radii, obeys \(\sup_{(P,m_0,m_1,p)\in\mathcal M_n}P\{|T(O^{(n)},m_0,m_1,p,r_{0n},r_{1n},r_{en})-\tau(P)|\ge c\rho_n\}\ge\delta_0\). Consequently \(\mathfrak R_n^{(1)}\ge c\delta_0\rho_n\) and \(\mathfrak R_n^{(2)}\ge c\sqrt{\delta_0}\rho_n\). Every fixed-sign law used by the fuzzy mixtures, rather than merely the mixtures themselves, belongs to \(\mathcal M_n\). Each of the four subexperiment families satisfies \(E_P[(g_1(X)-g_0(X))^2]\le M\) by regression-amplitude calibration within the applicable nuisance radius or a sufficiently small fixed constant.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: As written, the theorem quantifies over radius triples even when the model class is empty; then the displayed positive supremum lower bound is false. Nonemptiness is only a necessary well-posedness qualification, and it also yields the required boundary compatibility \(1-\eta_+>\lambda_0/2\) from the frozen shell and right-overlap assumptions.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: Uniformly over the bounded radius regime \( (r_{0n},r_{1n},r_{en})\in[0,\bar r]^3 \) for which \(\mathcal M_n\) is nonempty and over the fixed reservoir-rich shell constants, with every minimax infimum taken over \(T\in\mathcal T_n\) measurable in the observed sample and allowed to use \(m_0\), \(m_1\), \(p\), and the certified radii, \(\mathfrak R_n^{(1)}\asymp\rho_n\), \(\mathfrak R_n^{(2)}\asymp\rho_n\), and \(\mathfrak R_{n,\delta}^{(\mathrm{prob})}\asymp\rho_n\) for every fixed \(\delta\in(0,\delta_0]\). Thus the same \(\rho_n\) is the sharp frontier for absolute risk, root mean-squared risk, and fixed-probability error.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The frontier inherits the converse's necessary nonemptiness qualification; without it all three minimax definitions are degenerate and the claimed positive equivalences fail.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: For every fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1/4)\) and every admissible radius triple \( (r_{0n},r_{1n},r_{en})\in[0,\bar r]^3 \) for which \(\mathcal M_n\) is nonempty, a choice of \(K_{\alpha}\) depending only on the supplied radii and fixed class constants makes \(\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}\in\mathcal I_n\) uniformly honest: \(\inf_{(P,m_0,m_1,p)\in\mathcal M_n}P\{\tau(P)\in\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}\}\ge1-\alpha\), with \(\sup_{\mathcal M_n}E_P[\operatorname{length}(\mathcal C_{n,\alpha})]\le C_{\alpha}\rho_n\). Conversely every uniformly honest rule \(C_n\in\mathcal I_n\), including every rule using the public functions and certified radii, has worst-case expected length at least \(c_{\alpha}\rho_n\), so \(\mathfrak L_{n,\alpha}\asymp\rho_n\).
proposed_statement_changes.reason: For an empty class honesty is vacuous and a zero-length interval is admissible, contradicting the positive lower-length claim. The qualification is therefore necessary and propagates from the lower-bound experiment.

open_obligations.what_is_open: The smallest adaptation penalty and its matching lower bound when the tail exponent, both shell constants, and all three nuisance radii are unknown.
open_obligations.obstruction: The proved oracle threshold uses the unknown quantities in three competing scales. The frozen adaptation handle does not specify observable confidence bounds for the global approximation errors, and the fixed certificates used in the oracle proof cannot be recovered uniformly from a validation sample without additional structure on the public predictors. Honest interval adaptation also requires a between-class testing argument not supplied by the fixed-index lower families.
open_obligations.attempted: A dyadic Lepski comparison controls stochastic differences between clipped scores, but its deterministic clipping biases contain \(r_{1n}\lambda^{\kappa/2}\), \(r_{1n}r_{en}/\lambda\), and \(r_{0n}r_{en}\), none of which has a uniformly estimable upper certificate under the frozen model. Reusing empirical shell counts estimates the observed propensity tail only after controlling the unknown propensity approximation error, which is the same unidentified radius entering the choice.
open_obligations.partial_result: With \(\kappa\), \(c_-\), \(c_+\), and the certified radii supplied, thm:clipped-absolute-upper, lem:median-risk-upgrade, and thm:honest-interval-frontier attain risk and expected length of order \(\rho_n\), so the oracle adaptation penalty is \(1\). No claim about the unknown-index penalty follows from the frozen primitives.

proofs.proof_tex:
By the polynomial-radius specialization in the statement and the symbol declarations, \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(a_0,a_1,a_e\geq 0\).  Hence
\[
0<r_{jn}=n^{-a_j}\leq 1\leq \bar r,
\qquad j\in\{0,1,e\},
\]
so the three radius bounds required by the bounded-radius regime hold.

We first extract the polynomial order of every summand in \(\rho_n\).  Define, only within this proof,
\[
t_\kappa:=\frac{\kappa}{2}+(1-\kappa)a_1,
\qquad
u_\kappa:=a_1+\frac{\kappa}{2(\kappa+1)},
\qquad
w_\kappa:=a_1+\frac{\kappa a_e}{\kappa+2},
\qquad
c:=a_0+a_e.
\]
The definition of \(Q_\kappa\) and the equality \(r_{1n}=n^{-a_1}\) give, when \(0<\kappa<1\),
\[
Q_\kappa(n,r_{1n})
=n^{-1/2}\vee n^{-\kappa/2}(n^{-a_1})^{1-\kappa}
=n^{-1/2}\vee n^{-t_\kappa}.
\]
The remaining three terms in the definition of \(\rho_n\) satisfy
\[
r_{1n}n^{-\kappa/[2(\kappa+1)]}=n^{-u_\kappa},
\qquad
r_{1n}r_{en}^{\kappa/(\kappa+2)}=n^{-w_\kappa},
\qquad
r_{0n}r_{en}=n^{-c}.
\]
For \(n\geq1\), the largest of finitely many powers \(n^{-s}\) is the power having the smallest exponent.  Therefore Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}phase\mbox{-}exponent}\) gives, for \(0<\kappa<1\),
\[
\beta_\kappa=\min\{1/2,t_\kappa,u_\kappa,w_\kappa,c\}.
\]
For \(\kappa>1\), Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}tail\mbox{-}noise\mbox{-}rate}\) gives \(Q_\kappa(n,r_{1n})=n^{-1/2}\), and hence
\[
\beta_\kappa=\min\{1/2,u_\kappa,w_\kappa,c\}.
\]
In either case, the summand whose exponent equals \(\beta_\kappa\) supplies the lower bound, while each of the four summands in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}sharp\mbox{-}rate}\) is at most \(n^{-\beta_\kappa}\).  Thus
\[
n^{-\beta_\kappa}\leq \rho_n\leq 4n^{-\beta_\kappa},
\qquad \kappa\neq1.
\]

At \(\kappa=1\), put
\[
L_n:=\sqrt{1+\log_+(nr_{1n}^2)}.
\]
Then \(Q_1(n,r_{1n})=n^{-1/2}L_n\), \(L_n\geq1\), and
\[
\beta_1=\min\{1/2,a_1+1/4,a_1+a_e/3,c\}.
\]
The same comparison, now using \(L_n\geq1\), yields
\[
n^{-\beta_1}\leq \rho_n\leq4L_n n^{-\beta_1}.
\]
This proves the asserted polynomial order, including the stated possible boundary logarithm.

It remains to characterize strict deterioration relative to \(B\).  First suppose \(B\leq a_1\).  For \(0<\kappa<1\),
\[
t_\kappa=(1-\kappa)a_1+\kappa/2\geq B,
\]
because both \(a_1\) and \(1/2\) are at least \(B\).  For every \(\kappa>0\),
\[
u_\kappa\geq a_1\geq B,
\qquad
w_\kappa\geq a_1\geq B.
\]
Also \(1/2\geq B\) and \(c=a_0+a_e\geq B\) by the definition
\(B=\min\{1/2,a_1+a_e,a_0+a_e\}\).  Thus every entry defining \(\beta_\kappa\) is at least \(B\).  Conversely, if the minimum defining \(B\) is attained by \(1/2\) or by \(c\), that same entry occurs in \(\beta_\kappa\).  In the remaining case \(B=a_1+a_e\); the inequalities \(B\leq a_1\) and \(a_e\geq0\) then force \(a_e=0\) and \(B=a_1=w_\kappa\).  Hence
\[
\beta_\kappa=B
\]
whenever \(B\leq a_1\), proving that there is no polynomial deterioration in this case.

Now suppose \(B>a_1\), and set \(x:=B-a_1>0\) as in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}deterioration\mbox{-}threshold}\).  Since \(B\leq1/2\) and \(B\leq a_1+a_e\),
\[
0<x\leq 1/2-a_1,
\qquad
0<x\leq a_e.
\]
In particular, \(a_1<1/2\), the first denominator below is positive, and \(a_e-x\geq0\).  Define the three extended-real cutoffs
\[
A_1:=\frac{x}{1/2-a_1},
\qquad
A_2:=\frac{2x}{1-2x},
\qquad
A_3:=\frac{2x}{a_e-x},
\]
with a zero denominator interpreted as \(+\infty\), exactly as in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}deterioration\mbox{-}threshold}\).  Notice that \(A_1\leq1\).

The tail-noise exponent is present only for \(0<\kappa<1\), and direct subtraction gives
\[
t_\kappa<B
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\kappa(1/2-a_1)<x
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\kappa<A_1.
\]
Because \(A_1\leq1\), the condition \(0<\kappa<A_1\) automatically lies in the range where this entry is present.  For the empty-shell exponent, if \(x<1/2\), multiplication by the positive number \(2(\kappa+1)\) gives
\[
u_\kappa<B
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{\kappa}{2(\kappa+1)}<x
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\kappa(1-2x)<2x
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\kappa<A_2.
\]
If \(x=1/2\), the strict inequality \(\kappa/[2(\kappa+1)]<x\) holds for every finite \(\kappa>0\), and the convention \(A_2=+\infty\) gives the same equivalence.  Finally, if \(a_e>x\),
\[
w_\kappa<B
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{\kappa a_e}{\kappa+2}<x
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\kappa(a_e-x)<2x
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\kappa<A_3.
\]
If \(a_e=x\), then \(\kappa a_e/(\kappa+2)<a_e=x\) for every finite \(\kappa>0\), again agreeing with \(A_3=+\infty\).

The two entries \(1/2\) and \(c\) are at least \(B\) by definition.  Consequently, the preceding three displays exhaust all ways in which an entry of \(\beta_\kappa\) can be strictly smaller than \(B\).  Taking their union,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta_\kappa<B
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(\kappa<A_1)\ \text{or}\ (\kappa<A_2)\ \text{or}\ (\kappa<A_3)\\
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0<\kappa<\max\{A_1,A_2,A_3\}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0<\kappa<\kappa_\dagger,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equivalence is Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}deterioration\mbox{-}threshold}\).  The strict inequalities also show that a finite boundary \(\kappa=\kappa_\dagger\) is not part of the deterioration region.

For completeness, the logarithmic qualification at \(\kappa=1\) is exact.  Since \(r_{1n}=n^{-a_1}\),
\[
L_n=\sqrt{1+\log_+(n^{1-2a_1})}.
\]
If \(a_1\geq1/2\), then \(n^{1-2a_1}\leq1\) and \(L_n=1\).  If \(a_1<1/2\), then \(L_n\) is of order \(\sqrt{\log n}\).  When \(\beta_1<1/2\), writing \(d:=1/2-\beta_1>0\) shows
\[
\frac{n^{-1/2}L_n}{n^{-\beta_1}}=n^{-d}L_n\longrightarrow0;
\]
indeed, after setting \(s=\log n\), the bound \(e^{ds}\geq (ds)^2/2\) proves the limit.  Hence the logarithm does not change the leading rate in that case.  When \(\beta_1=1/2\), all three non-noise terms are at most \(n^{-1/2}\), so
\[
n^{-1/2}L_n\leq\rho_n\leq4n^{-1/2}L_n.
\]
Thus the boundary factor changes a leading root-\(n\) rate exactly when \(a_1<1/2\) and \(\beta_1=1/2\), which in particular proves the necessary condition stated in the proposition.

Finally,
\[
\frac{d}{d\kappa}u_\kappa=\frac{1}{2(\kappa+1)^2}>0,
\qquad
\lim_{\kappa\to\infty}u_\kappa=a_1+1/2\geq1/2\geq B.
\]
Therefore the empty-shell channel has no surviving deterioration in the fast-tail limit; any deterioration at finite \(\kappa\) is already exactly accounted for by the cutoff \(A_2\) above.

Fix \(\kappa>0\).  Suppose, toward a contradiction, that a quadruple
\((P,m_0,m_1,p)\) belongs to
\(\mathcal M_n\cap\mathcal M_n^{\mathrm{reg}}\).  Set
\[
u_\star=\frac12\min\{\lambda_0,\eta_-\}.
\]
The declared ranges \(\lambda_0\in(0,1)\) and \(\eta_-\in(0,1)\) imply
\(0<u_\star\le\lambda_0\) and \(u_\star<\eta_-\).  Membership in
\(\mathcal M_n\), by \(\mathrm{def:public\mbox{-}weak\mbox{-}overlap\mbox{-}class}\),
imposes \(\mathrm{ass:uniform\mbox{-}shell}\).  Consequently,
\[
P\!\left\{\frac{u_\star}{2}<e(X)\le u_\star\right\}
\ge c_-u_\star^{\kappa}>0,
\]
where strict positivity follows from \(c_->0\), \(u_\star>0\), and
\(\kappa>0\).  On the other hand, membership in
\(\mathcal M_n^{\mathrm{reg}}\), by
\(\mathrm{def:regular\mbox{-}overlap\mbox{-}class}\), imposes
\(\mathrm{ass:uniform\mbox{-}overlap\mbox{-}comparator}\), hence
\(P\{e(X)\ge\eta_-\}=1\).  Because \(u_\star<\eta_-\),
\[
\left\{\frac{u_\star}{2}<e(X)\le u_\star\right\}
\subseteq\{e(X)<\eta_-\},
\]
so the probability in the preceding display is zero, a contradiction.  Thus
\[
\mathcal M_n\cap\mathcal M_n^{\mathrm{reg}}=\varnothing.
\]

Now fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) and
\((r_{0n},r_{1n},r_{en})\in[0,\bar r]^3\).  Since a sample size is positive,
\(n>0\).  For every \(\kappa>1\),
\(\mathrm{def:tail\mbox{-}noise\mbox{-}rate}\) gives
\[
Q_\kappa(n,r_{1n})=n^{-1/2}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\frac{\kappa}{2(\kappa+1)}\longrightarrow\frac12,
\qquad
\frac{\kappa}{\kappa+2}\longrightarrow1.
\]
Continuity of \(a\mapsto n^{-a}\) therefore yields
\[
r_{1n}n^{-\kappa/[2(\kappa+1)]}
\longrightarrow r_{1n}n^{-1/2}.
\]
If \(r_{en}>0\), continuity of \(a\mapsto r_{en}^a\) gives
\(r_{en}^{\kappa/(\kappa+2)}\to r_{en}\); if \(r_{en}=0\), both sides are
zero because \(\kappa/(\kappa+2)>0\).  Hence in all cases
\[
r_{1n}r_{en}^{\kappa/(\kappa+2)}\longrightarrow r_{1n}r_{en}.
\]
Substitution into \(\mathrm{def:sharp\mbox{-}rate}\), followed by passage to
the limit in this finite sum, proves
\[
\lim_{\kappa\to\infty}\rho_n
=(1+r_{1n})n^{-1/2}+r_{1n}r_{en}+r_{0n}r_{en}.
\]

For the asserted uniform comparison, put
\[
A_n=r_{1n}r_{en}+r_{0n}r_{en}\ge0,
\qquad
B_n=n^{-1/2}+A_n>0.
\]
The radius restriction in either class gives \(0\le r_{1n}\le\bar r\).
Therefore
\[
B_n
\le (1+r_{1n})n^{-1/2}+A_n
\le (1+\bar r)n^{-1/2}+A_n
\le (1+\bar r)B_n.
\]
The constants \(1\) and \(1+\bar r\) do not depend on \(n\) or on the three
radii, which proves
\[
(1+r_{1n})n^{-1/2}+r_{1n}r_{en}+r_{0n}r_{en}
\asymp n^{-1/2}+r_{1n}r_{en}+r_{0n}r_{en}
\]
uniformly over \(r_{1n}\le\bar r\).  The cited comparator results
\(\mathrm{lem:jin\mbox{-}syrgkanis\mbox{-}regular\mbox{-}benchmark}\) and
\(\mathrm{lem:bonvini\mbox{-}et\mbox{-}al\mbox{-}regular\mbox{-}benchmark}\)
identify the final expression as the published bounded-overlap
public-function benchmark.  Since the first part proves that the two model
classes are disjoint, this limiting calculation is a fast-tail reduction of
rate formulas between distinct experiments and cannot be a class-inclusion
argument.

proposed.statement: For every fixed \(\kappa>0\), \(\mathcal M_n\cap\mathcal M_n^{\mathrm{reg}}=\varnothing\): ass:uniform-shell places positive mass below every positive propensity threshold, whereas ass:uniform-overlap-comparator imposes \(e(X)\ge\eta_-\) almost surely. For fixed \(n\) and \((r_{0n},r_{1n},r_{en})\in[0,\bar r]^3\), \(\lim_{\kappa\to\infty}\rho_n=(1+r_{1n})n^{-1/2}+r_{1n}r_{en}+r_{0n}r_{en}\asymp n^{-1/2}+r_{1n}r_{en}+r_{0n}r_{en}\), uniformly under \(r_{1n}\le\bar r\). The last display is the known bounded-overlap public-function benchmark of JinSyrgkanis2024StructureAgnosticDR and BonviniKennedyDukesBalakrishnan2024StructureAgnosticATE. Thus the relation is a fast-tail rate reduction between distinct experiments, not a class inclusion.
proposed.justification: This known-comparator proposition records both the strict class separation and the exact surviving treated empty-shell term needed for a valid standard-case check.
proposed.gap: JinSyrgkanis2024StructureAgnosticDR, Theorem 1 and Remark 2, and BonviniKennedyDukesBalakrishnan2024StructureAgnosticATE, Section 2, establish the bounded-overlap product-rate benchmark; JinSyrgkanis2025GeneralLinearFunctionalLowerBounds, Section 6.1 and the conclusion, identifies weak-overlap distribution shift as an open direction. The new theorem concerns the separate dyadic-shell experiment rather than reproving that benchmark.
